components.gap: Source s.1 (author PDF pp.1-4): the simple unary predicate model SU(n,p) with p=p(n), the YES example and the p=c/n limit 1-e^{-c}, the almost-surely/almost-never and threshold-function definitions (threshold n^{-1}), the zero-one theorem for p(n)>>n^{-1} and 1-p(n)>>n^{-1}, its proof via the almost sure theory T (completeness via countable models and the Duplicator strategy), and the failure boundary near the thresholds must be written with complete proofs; the handbook only has the uniform p=1/2 monadic count lemma of Fagin1976, a weaker fixed special case.

Only G(n,p) with p fixed (and G(n,1/2)) is defined. Source s.2 (pp.4-6) owes: G(n,p(n)) with p a function of n; threshold functions; the worked threshold examples (K4 at n^{-2/3}, triangle at n^{-1}, no isolated vertices at n^{-1}ln n, every two vertices have a common neighbour at n^{-1/2}ln^{1/2}n, the path example at n^{-2/3}ln^{1/3}n) with their justifications; and the Shelah-Spencer zero-one law for p=n^{-alpha}, alpha irrational in (0,1), with exact hypotheses.

Only one-new-vertex extension axioms at fixed density are present. Source s.3 (pp.6-8) owes: rooted graphs (R,H) and the extension statement Ext(R,H) with parameters r,v,e; dense/sparse via the sign of v-alpha e (irrationality making a strict dichotomy); rigid and safe extensions and subextensions; the worked alpha=pi/7 examples; and the claim, with its justification, that Ext(R,H) holds almost surely iff (R,H) is safe.

Source s.4 (pp.8-9) owes the t-closure cl_t(X) for irrational alpha: the algorithmic definition via rigid extensions with at most t nonroots, the equivalent formulation, the almost-sure bound on closure sizes, and their complete proofs; none is on the handbook route.

Source s.5 (pp.9-12) owes the almost sure theory T for p=n^{-alpha}: its schema (safe extension statements and nonexistence of dense configurations), the proof that each member holds almost surely, the Duplicator strategy via closures (sequence t_0,...,t_u, isomorphic SMALL-closures) proving completeness, and the resulting zero-one law; none is on the handbook route.

The constant-p G(n,p) extension schema, witness probability p^r(1-p)^s, union bound and zero-one law are proved, but only as a Fagin1976 presentation by compactness and back-and-forth. Spencer's s.6 (pp.12-13) presentation is not supplied: no SRC-050 citation or locators, no Alice's Restaurant property, and no completeness proof by Duplicator's staying-alive strategy in EHR[G,G';t] through the s.14 completeness corollary.

Only the constant-p countable model (the Rado graph, aleph_0-categorical) is present. Source s.7 (pp.13-15) owes: the argument that an almost sure theory has no finite models and hence a countable model; the aleph_0-categoricity argument as given for the Alice's Restaurant theory; and the analysis of the countable models of the p=n^{-alpha} theory (not aleph_0-categorical; construction via rigid extensions and finite closures, with the stated examples), with complete proofs.

Source s.8 (pp.15-16) owes the dynamic view: the function f_A(alpha) giving the limiting truth value of A at p=n^{-alpha}, its definition independent of probability calculation, and its stated properties with proofs; absent.

Source s.9 (pp.16-18) owes infinite spectra via almost sure encoding: the spectrum of A (the alpha where f_A is discontinuous / no zero-one law), the encoding constructions (e.g. parity of common-neighbourhood counts), and the theorem that a first-order spectrum can be infinite, with its proof; absent.
Source s.10 (pp.18-19) owes the jump condition on spectra, with the t_0..t_u intervals, the worked alpha example, and its proof; absent.
Source s.11 (pp.19-22) owes the complexity condition on spectra (levels of possible configurations and the complexity bound), with its construction and proof; absent.
Source s.12 (pp.22-25) owes nonconvergence via almost sure encoding: a first-order sentence whose probability fails to converge in the stated regime, with the construction and proof; absent.
Source s.13 (pp.25-26) owes the theorem that no first-order A almost surely represents evenness of n, with its encoding/circuit argument and proof; absent.

The game definition and the cited game theorem are present. Source s.14 (pp.26-27) items absent: the isolated-vertex worked example (Spoiler wins in two rounds); the corollary that elementary equivalence holds iff Duplicator wins EHR[G,H;t] for every t, with the warning that this differs from the infinite game; and the corollary that a consistent theory without finite models is complete iff Duplicator wins EHR[G,H;t] on every two countable models for every t, with its written proof; no SRC-050 citation.

Source s.15 'About the references' (pp.27-28) owes the attribution and literature guidance: surveys (Compton, Winkler, Lynch, Spencer), origin of the Ehrenfeucht game, Glebskii et al. and Fagin for p=1/2, Erdos-Renyi and Bollobas, Shelah-Spencer for n^{-alpha} and the game/syntactic/countable-model treatments, other random models and stronger logics, Luczak-Spencer near-characterization, Spencer-Tardos conditions on f_A; absent.
